Last updated November 14, 2026.

Georgia property tax is assessed by the county board of tax assessors and collected by the county tax commissioner.

What the official sources say

  • Owner may appeal within 45 days of the date the Assessment Notice was mailed; grounds include taxability, value, uniformity and denial of an exemption. (Filing a Property Tax Appeal | Department of Revenue (O.C.G.A. 48-5-311); source)
  • The written appeal is filed with the County Board of Tax Assessors (not DOR) and the owner picks one of three routes: Board of Equalization, Hearing Officer, or Arbitrator. (Filing a Property Tax Appeal | Department of Revenue (O.C.G.A. 48-5-311); source)
  • Hearing Officer route is only for non-homestead real property valued over $500,000. (Filing a Property Tax Appeal | Department of Revenue (O.C.G.A. 48-5-311); source)
  • Appeal to superior court must be noticed within 30 days of the decision; taxes must be paid in the amount of the last year's taxes before the court hears it. (Filing a Property Tax Appeal | Department of Revenue (O.C.G.A. 48-5-311); source)
  • Fair market value is the amount a knowledgeable buyer would pay and a willing seller accept in an arm's length bona fide sale; assessed value is 40% of fair market value. (Property Tax - Real and Personal Property - FAQ | Department of Revenue; source)
  • All property is to be returned and assessed at fair market value every year as of January 1 (O.C.G.A. 48-5-6, 48-5-2). (Property Tax - Real and Personal Property - FAQ | Department of Revenue; source)
  • HB 581 (Rep. Blackmon) passed March 28, 2024 and was signed April 18, 2024; it provides a statewide floating homestead exemption (legible parts of brief), requiring ratification of a constitutional amendment on the Nov 5, 2024 ballot, with local governments able to opt out by March 1, 2025. (HB 581 Property Tax Reform policy brief | Georgia House Budget and Research Office (PDF text partly garbled; inflation-cap detail not relied on); source)
  • DOR says taxpayers may now apply for homestead exemption beyond April 1, up to the end of the 45-day assessment appeal window. (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • DeKalb: sales are on the first Tuesday of the month at the courthouse steps (12:00 p.m. or sooner), with notice published once a week for four weeks in the county legal organ. (Tax Sales | DeKalb County Tax Commissioner; source)
  • Cobb: sales are the first Tuesday of the month between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.; the tax deed (not a lien) is sold to the highest bidder; payment in full by cash or certified check. (Tax Sales | Cobb County Tax Commissioner; source)

Georgia homeowners can claim a homestead exemption on their legal residence, and the Department of Revenue explains the rules.

What the official sources say

  • A homeowner is generally entitled to homestead exemption if they owned and lived in the home as legal residence as of January 1 of the tax year (O.C.G.A. 48-5-40). (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Applications are filed with the county tax commissioner (or assessor in some counties); the historic deadline is April 1. (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • DOR states taxpayers can now apply beyond April 1, up to the end of the 45-day window to appeal their notice of assessment. (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Standard state homestead exemption is $2,000, deducted from the 40% assessed value (O.C.G.A. 48-5-44). (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • State senior exemptions include $4,000 for age 65+ with income up to $10,000 (48-5-47) and a floating inflation-proof exemption for age 62+ with income up to $30,000 (48-5-47.1). (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Disabled veteran exemption: greater of $32,500 or the federal maximum; DOR lists $121,812 for 2025. (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Many counties offer larger local exemptions, including valuation freezes; DOR lists counties such as Cobb, DeKalb, Fulton, Gwinnett, Cherokee, Forsyth. (Property Tax Homestead Exemptions | Department of Revenue; source)

Most Georgia foreclosures use a power of sale and happen on the first Tuesday of the month.

What the official sources say

  • Georgia is a non-judicial foreclosure state: the lender can foreclose without filing suit; procedures are in O.C.G.A. 44-14-162 through 44-14-162.4. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • Notice of intent to foreclose must be sent to the borrower at least 30 days before the proposed sale, in writing, by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, and include a copy of the sale advertisement. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • The notice must include name, address and phone of someone with authority to negotiate, amend and modify the loan terms. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • The sale must be advertised in the county's official legal organ for four consecutive weeks before the sale. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • Foreclosure sales are held on the courthouse steps on the first Tuesday of the month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • After sale the lender may sue for a deficiency (difference between sale price and debt owed); AG notes this goes before the courts. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • The foreclosure purchaser may file a dispossessory action to remove the borrower after sale. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • Alternatives listed by the AG: cure default, short sale, deed in lieu, bankruptcy; a bankruptcy petition filed before the sale stays a non-judicial foreclosure. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • Foreclosure sales under power of sale occur on the first Tuesday of the month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. on the courthouse steps. (Mortgage and Foreclosure Information | Office of the Attorney General; source)
  • Cobb County tax sales are held the first Tuesday of the month at the Superior Court Plaza between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.; if a holiday, the first Wednesday. (Tax Sales | Cobb County Tax Commissioner; source)
  • DeKalb County tax sales are on the first Tuesday of any month on the courthouse steps at 12:00 p.m. or sooner. (Tax Sales | DeKalb County Tax Commissioner; source)
  • Tax sale notices run once a week for four weeks in the county legal organ before the sale. (Tax Sales | DeKalb County Tax Commissioner; source)

content:

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Quit claim (non-warranty) deeds can transfer property or clear titles but give no warranty that the grantor owns or has rights to transfer the property. (Transfer Property with a Quit Claim Deed | Georgia.gov; source)
  • Georgia.gov advises getting title insurance and consulting a real estate attorney before accepting a quit claim deed. (Transfer Property with a Quit Claim Deed | Georgia.gov; source)
  • Warranty and limited warranty deeds are usually more reliable because they include a covenant of ownership. (Transfer Property with a Quit Claim Deed | Georgia.gov; source)
  • A quit claim deed alone no longer gives ownership after 7 years of uncontested use; more documentation is required. (Transfer Property with a Quit Claim Deed | Georgia.gov; source)
  • After payment, the clerk or deputy attaches a certification that the tax has been paid. (PT61 eFiling in Georgia | GSCCCA; source)
  • PT-61 is completed online through the GSCCCA portal and a copy is printed and filed with the clerk along with the deed documents. (PT61 eFiling in Georgia | GSCCCA; source)

What we could not confirm

  • A county by county recording fee table was not retrieved.

Georgia quitclaim deed FAQ

Where do I record a Georgia deed?

With the Clerk of Superior Court of the county where the property is located.

What does a Georgia quitclaim deed actually transfer?

A Georgia quitclaim deed passes whatever interest the signer holds in the property and promises nothing about it. The Georgia Department of Revenue puts it plainly in its deed course material: if the grantor holds fee simple title, the grantee receives fee simple title, and if the grantor holds nothing, the grantee receives nothing.

That is the whole difference from a warranty deed. A warranty deed carries a covenant that the grantor really owns the land, which is why Georgia.gov calls warranty and limited warranty deeds usually the most reliable, though harder to negotiate. A quitclaim deed is easier to get from a seller, and the same page tells anyone accepting one to get protection such as title insurance first.

Because nothing is guaranteed, the deed is a tool for specific jobs rather than a general way to sell a house at full market confidence.

When do Georgia owners use a quitclaim deed?

Owners reach for a quitclaim deed when the title is murky or when no sale price is involved. The Department of Revenue course text lists the common uses.

  • Settling the affairs of a deceased owner when the quality of title is uncertain.
  • Resolving a boundary dispute where the property line is not clear.
  • Moving a spouse's interest to the other spouse, which transfers whatever interest the signer had.
  • Cancelling a security deed after a loan is paid, especially when the original security deed is lost.
  • Moving title after an involuntary sale, such as a sale on a judgment or a tax lien.

That last use is built into the tax sale statutes. When property is redeemed after a tax sale, O.C.G.A. 48-4-44 requires the tax sale purchaser to give the owner a quitclaim deed naming who paid the redemption money. Our Georgia tax sale guide covers how that redemption works.

What makes a quitclaim deed valid and recordable in Georgia?

A deed to land must be an original, written, and signed by the maker. O.C.G.A. 44-5-30 adds that it must be attested by an officer and by one other witness, and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's representative. The Department of Revenue course text summarizes this as two witnesses, one of whom is a notary public.

No special form is required. Under 44-5-33, a deed that makes the transaction clear is not defeated by a want of form, so a quitclaim deed can be short. The deed still needs consideration, with one exception: the same course text notes that a deed of gift does not require valuable consideration.

Recording adds a few mechanical rules under 44-2-14. The instrument must be an original that is attested or acknowledged as the law requires, and the name and mailing address of the natural person to receive it back must be printed or typed at the top of the first page. Skipping that return address does not by itself erase the filing, but clerks expect it.

A deed is recorded with the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the land sits. Ask that clerk for current recording fees and any local formatting preferences.

How does transfer tax work on a quitclaim deed?

Georgia will not record a deed until the real estate transfer tax has been paid. The Department of Revenue says the clerk, or a deputy, then attaches a certification that the tax was paid. The Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority adds that this tax is an excise tax and not a property tax.

The Department of Revenue prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part of $1,000, plus 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100, based on the sale price. The person who executes the deed, or the person for whose benefit it is executed, owes the tax. The seller is liable, though contracts often shift the cost to the buyer.

Georgia law also requires the PT-61 declaration. The Authority runs a free online filing system with no account needed: you complete the form on its site, print a reference copy, and file it with the clerk along with the deed. No signatures are needed on the electronic form.

  • A PT-61 is required whenever ownership changes, even when no money moves, such as removing a name from a deed.
  • The Authority lists four categories that need no PT-61: security deeds, releases of security interest, leases other than a lease for years, and affidavits that do not transfer property.
  • Other exemptions from paying the tax still require the form to be filed.
  • A property that crosses county lines needs a deed and a PT-61 in each county, with the value pro-rated.
  • A transfer-on-death deed needs no PT-61 when recorded, but one is required after the owner dies and the beneficiary files an affidavit accepting the property.

For questions about what is taxable or exempt, the Department of Revenue says to ask the Clerk of Superior Court in your county.

What are the steps from signing to recording?

The sequence below follows the statutes and agency pages already cited. Each step is the owner's job unless a closing attorney handles it.

Georgia quitclaim deed steps and the official source for each
StepWhat happensSource
1. Prepare the deedOriginal, written, signed by the grantor; return address at top of page oneO.C.G.A. 44-5-30 and 44-2-14 in the Department of Revenue course text
2. Witness itAttested by an officer plus one other witnessO.C.G.A. 44-5-30
3. Complete the PT-61Filed online with the Clerks' Authority, then a reference copy is printedClerks' Authority PT-61 help pages
4. Pay transfer taxPaid before recording; clerk certifies payment on the deedDepartment of Revenue transfer tax page
5. Record the deedFiled with the Clerk of Superior Court in the county of the landDepartment of Revenue transfer tax page

Does a seven year rule make a quitclaim deed enough to own the house?

No. Georgia.gov states that in the past a quitclaim deed gave full ownership after seven years of uncontested use, even when the person who gave you the deed was not the real owner, and that this is no longer so simple. More documentation than the deed alone is needed to be recognized as the owner.

The seven year period still appears in the law of prescription. The Department of Revenue course text explains that O.C.G.A. 44-5-164 allows title by prescription after seven years when the possessor holds a flawed written document, called color of title, and possession was public, continuous, exclusive, peaceable, and not merely permissive. Without color of title, 44-5-163 requires twenty years. Our Georgia adverse possession guide goes deeper on those periods.

For a seller, the practical point is that a quitclaim deed from a doubtful source does not cure a title problem on its own. A buyer or title insurer will look at the chain of title behind it.

How does a quitclaim deed fit into selling a Georgia house?

A quitclaim deed can move title between family members or clear a name before a sale, but a buyer receives no promise from it. Title insurance, which Georgia.gov recommends, is how buyers cover that gap, and insurers will examine the records behind the deed.

If you inherited a home with several heirs, or you are removing a former spouse from title, a quitclaim deed signed by that person may be the missing piece before you can list or sell. Each person with an interest usually has to sign for the buyer to receive the whole property. A Georgia real estate attorney can tell you whether a quitclaim deed, a warranty deed, or a court process fits your situation, and Georgia.gov points to the State Bar of Georgia for finding one.

More questions about Georgia Quitclaim Deed

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in Georgia?

With the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the land is located. Bring the original deed and the PT-61 reference copy, and have the transfer tax paid so the clerk can certify it.

Is a PT-61 form required if I am only adding or removing a name?

Yes. The Clerks' Authority says a PT-61 is required whenever ownership is changed, even without a payment, except for security deeds, releases of security interest, leases other than leases for years, and affidavits. Ask the clerk whether the tax itself is exempt.

Does a quitclaim deed protect the person who receives it?

No. It gives the grantee only what the grantor owns, with no warranty. Georgia.gov recommends title insurance and says a real estate attorney can help before you accept one.

Who pays the Georgia real estate transfer tax?

The seller is liable under the Department of Revenue's description, but a sales contract can assign the cost to the buyer. On a gift or family transfer, ask the Clerk of Superior Court whether an exemption applies.

Can I use a quitclaim deed to get my house back after a tax sale?

If you redeem the property after a tax sale, the purchaser must give you a quitclaim deed under O.C.G.A. 48-4-44. It should name the person who paid the redemption money, and it is recorded with the county clerk.

  • Property taxes are normally due December 20 in most counties, but due dates vary by county. (Property Tax - Real and Personal Property - FAQ | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Real estate transfer tax is an excise tax on transactions where title to real property is transferred from seller to buyer. (Real Estate Transfer Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Rate: $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part, plus 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part, based on the sale price. (Real Estate Transfer Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • The tax must be paid by the person who executes the deed or the person for whose use or benefit it is executed; the seller is liable, though parties often agree in the contract that the buyer pays. (Real Estate Transfer Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • The tax must be paid before a deed can be recorded with the clerk of superior court; the clerk then attaches a certification of payment. (Real Estate Transfer Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • The PT-61 transfer tax declaration is filed online through the GSCCCA; only one PT-61 is filed per applicable deed. (PT61 eFiling in Georgia | GSCCCA; source)
  • Questions about taxability and exemptions are directed by DOR to the county Clerk of Superior Court. (Real Estate Transfer Tax | Department of Revenue; source)
  • Statutory range cited by DOR: O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10. (Real Estate Transfer Tax | Department of Revenue; source)

What the official sources say

What we could not confirm

  • Statute text for some tax sale rules appears only on non-official sites.

Georgia tax lien FAQ

Can I stop a tax sale?

Paying the delinquent amount or selling before the sale can pay the tax from the proceeds. Ask the county tax commissioner for exact figures.

What is a tax lien on a Georgia house?

In Georgia a tax lien on real estate is called a fi. fa., short for fieri facias, and it is also called a tax execution. The Gwinnett County Tax Commissioner describes it as a claim on the property that lets the tax commissioner or the sheriff take whatever action the law allows to collect overdue taxes, and the first step toward a tax sale.

Some states package these liens and sell them to investors. Metro Atlanta counties work differently. Cobb County's tax commissioner states that the office does not sell tax liens and instead sells tax deeds at auction, and Gwinnett says it does not transfer liens in bulk to third-party investors. What a buyer gets at a Georgia sale is a tax deed, covered in our tax sale guide.

When does unpaid property tax turn into a lien?

The trigger is delinquency, and counties word it a little differently. DeKalb County says accounts with a balance after December 31 are subject to a lien, and that partial payments are accepted but penalties and interest keep accruing on what remains. Cobb County says unpaid taxes after the October 15 due date are subject to levy and tax sale.

Gwinnett adds a notice step for homes and land: for real property, the tax commissioner must send the owner a 30-day notice before filing the lien. Personal property liens can be filed any time after the account is delinquent.

Due dates differ by county and by year, so look at your own bill or ask the county tax commissioner before assuming a date.

What happens after the lien is filed?

A filed lien does not take the house by itself. The usual path runs through a levy, an advertisement, and an auction.

  • Lien filed. A filing fee is added to the account, and the lien stays until the taxes are paid in full.
  • Levy. Gwinnett explains that for real property a levy can be a posted sign. It does not change ownership and does not take away the owner's right to live there. Once levied, only certified funds are accepted and partial payments stop.
  • Selection for sale. Costs for title research and advertising are added. The owner can still pay everything owed to stop the sale.
  • Auction. The sale happens on the first Tuesday of a month, and the winning bidder receives a tax deed.

DeKalb notes that a lien may show up on credit reports even though the office does not report to credit agencies, and Gwinnett warns that a lien can complicate real property closings.

How do DeKalb, Cobb and Gwinnett handle delinquent accounts?

The same state statutes apply everywhere, but each tax commissioner publishes its own practices. The comparison below uses only what each county's own page states.

Delinquent tax practices published by three metro Atlanta tax commissioners
CountyLien timingSale location and payment
DeKalbBalances outstanding after December 31 are subject to a lienCourthouse steps, first Tuesday, April through December; cash, bank cashier's check or bank wire once scheduled
CobbUnpaid after the October 15 due date is subject to levy and saleSuperior Court Plaza on the first Tuesday of planned months; cash or certified check; tax deeds only
Gwinnett30-day notice for real property before a lien is filedIn front of the Justice and Administration Center in Lawrenceville; certified funds only

Other counties set their own routines, so call the tax commissioner for the parcel in question.

What charges get added on top of the unpaid tax?

The balance grows at each stage, which is why paying early is cheaper. DeKalb's conditions of sale list the opening bid as the original taxes, the late payment penalty, interest, the fi. fa. cost, an execution fee and other legal costs and fees the law allows.

  • Gwinnett adds a fi. fa. filing fee when the lien is filed.
  • Gwinnett adds levy costs and fees once a property is levied upon.
  • Once a property is picked for sale, Gwinnett adds costs for title research and advertising.
  • DeKalb keeps adding penalties and interest to any balance left after a partial payment.

Ask the tax commissioner for an itemized payoff before you list the house, so the figure in your sales contract matches what the county will actually require on the closing date.

Who is named on the lien if I sold the house during the year?

Georgia taxes accrue in full on January 1, so the January 1 owner carries the bill. Gwinnett's tax commissioner explains that both the seller and the new owner may receive a bill, and that a lien for unpaid taxes goes in the January 1 owner's name unless proof of the buyer's assumption is filed in time.

Three things must be in place within 90 days of the payment due date: acceptable proof that the purchaser assumed liability, a deed in the new owner's name, and proper recording of that deed. Wording matters. Gwinnett's examples of unacceptable contract language include general promises to prorate or to adjust between buyer and seller. Acceptable wording assigns the property tax liability to the purchaser, who agrees to pay it in full by the due date.

If the tax is paid on time, no paperwork is needed. If you are selling, ask the closing attorney to use clear assumption language and confirm the new deed is recorded.

How can I clear a lien before selling?

Payment of the outstanding taxes plus the fees, penalties and interest gets the lien marked satisfied, according to DeKalb. If a closing is coming, ask the tax commissioner for a payoff figure good through the closing date, and have the title company pay it from the proceeds.

Watch the payment form. After a property is scheduled for sale, DeKalb accepts only cash, bank-issued cashier's check or bank wire, and Gwinnett requires certified funds once the property is levied. Personal checks and cards will not do at that stage.

An older tax problem can also sit behind a current bill. DeKalb's delinquent report covers taxes due within the last seven years, and it warns that opening bids at a sale include all prior year taxes, so ask the office for anything older than that.

Is there a court-based alternative to a tax sale?

Yes. Georgia's judicial in rem foreclosure statutes, O.C.G.A. 48-4-75 through 48-4-81, let a county or city adopt a court process for delinquent property tax. A tax collector may not start one until 12 months after the taxes first became delinquent.

The proceeding enforces the lien only and does not create personal liability for the owner. Any interested party can redeem before the sale by paying the redemption amount. After a sale the owner has 60 days to redeem, and any amount bid above the minimum is placed with the superior court for distribution to interested parties, including the owner. Not every county has adopted this process, so ask the county tax commissioner which procedure applies.

More questions about Georgia Tax Liens

Can a Georgia tax lien stop me from selling my house?

It complicates the sale but does not block it. Gwinnett says liens can affect real property closing procedures, so the lien is normally paid off at closing and then marked satisfied.

Does a tax lien mean I lose my home right away?

No. A lien is the first step toward a sale. Gwinnett describes a real property levy as a posted sign that does not change ownership or the owner's right to live there, and a buyer at a sale still must wait out the redemption period.

Can I make partial payments on delinquent property tax?

DeKalb and Gwinnett both accept partial payments, but DeKalb says penalties and interest continue on the remainder, and Gwinnett says partial payments do not necessarily keep a property out of levy and sale. Once Gwinnett levies, partial payments stop.

Will a tax lien hurt my credit?

It can. DeKalb says its office does not report to credit agencies but that a lien may still appear on credit reports. Paying the balance in full gets the lien marked satisfied.

Do Georgia counties sell tax liens to investors?

Cobb states that it does not sell tax liens and instead sells tax deeds at auction, and Gwinnett says it does not transfer liens in bulk to investors. Ask your own county tax commissioner how it handles sales.

Georgia Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the First Tuesday Sale

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Georgia Tax Sales sale
  • Turn the Georgia Tax Sales offer down and you owe us nothing

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Redemption price = bid amount + taxes paid later by purchaser + special assessments + 20% premium for the first year or fraction, 10% for each additional year or fraction, plus sheriff and advertising costs. (Tax Sales | Cobb County Tax Commissioner; source)
  • After 12 months the purchaser may foreclose the right of redemption by serving notice on all parties of record; Cobb also requires publication once a week for four consecutive weeks. (Tax Sales | Cobb County Tax Commissioner; source)
  • The tax sale purchaser cannot take possession, improve the property or evict tenants before the redemption right is foreclosed (Cobb). (Tax Sales | Cobb County Tax Commissioner; source)
Selling in Georgia?
We buy Georgia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Statute text appears on non-official sites, so county pages are cited instead.

Georgia tax sale FAQ

Can I redeem after a tax sale?

County tax commissioner pages describe a redemption period and premium. Confirm exact amounts with your county.

How does a Georgia tax sale work?

A Georgia tax sale is a public auction of a delinquent property after a tax lien has been issued and the property has been advertised. The winning bidder receives a tax deed, and the owner keeps a right to buy the property back. Sales run under O.C.G.A. 48-3-1 and 48-4-1 and following, as the DeKalb County conditions of sale state.

The county sets the calendar. DeKalb holds sales on the first Tuesday of the month from April through December on the courthouse steps in Decatur. Cobb holds them on the first Tuesday of the months it plans a sale, moving to Wednesday if Tuesday is a holiday. Gwinnett says it generally holds sales in only a few selected months.

Opening bids are the unpaid taxes plus penalties, interest, and costs. Georgia sells the deed, and the lien itself is not what changes hands, a point Cobb stresses by stating that it sells tax deeds and does not sell tax liens.

What does a bidder have to do on sale day?

Registration comes first. Cobb requires pre-registration for each sale and issues bidder cards between 9:00 and 10:00 a.m. on the day, against a photo ID. DeKalb requires registration for each sale as well, either online beforehand or in person that morning.

  • Payment. Cobb wants payment in full when the sale ends, by cash or certified check. DeKalb's conditions require cash, a cashier's check or a certified check from an insured institution within one hour after the sale ends.
  • Failure to pay. DeKalb says an unpaid bid goes back up for resale the same afternoon, and the defaulting bidder may owe the difference or be barred from later sales.
  • Unsold parcels. Cobb may re-auction properties that drew no bid at 3 p.m. that afternoon.
  • Buyer beware. DeKalb's conditions state that the doctrine of caveat emptor applies to every tax sale.

For an owner, the same details matter in reverse: once a sale is scheduled, DeKalb accepts only cash, bank cashier's checks or bank wires, and Gwinnett accepts only certified funds.

How long can the owner take the property back?

At least 12 months, and often longer. O.C.G.A. 48-4-40 lets the defendant in the execution, or anyone with a right, title, interest or lien in the property, redeem within 12 months of the sale, and after that until the right is cut off by the statutory notice.

Georgia's redemption price is set by 48-4-42. The table below lists the pieces as the Department of Revenue course text prints them for sales after July 1, 2002.

What the redemption payment includes under O.C.G.A. 48-4-42
ComponentRule as printed
BidThe amount paid at the tax sale, as shown in the tax deed
Later taxesAny taxes the purchaser paid after the sale
Special assessmentsAny special assessments on the property
Premium20 percent for the first year or fraction of a year since the sale, then 10 percent for each additional year or fraction of a year
Notice costsSheriff's cost for serving the notice and publication costs, if redemption comes more than 30 days after the foreclosure notice
Association sumsFor sales after July 1, 2016, certain amounts paid to a property owners', condominium or homeowners' association

Payment goes to the purchaser in lawful United States money. Cobb adds that the tax sale purchaser is responsible for working out the redemption amount, so ask the purchaser or the tax commissioner for a written figure.

Can the purchaser move in right after the sale?

No. Cobb's tax commissioner states that the purchaser gets a tax deed but cannot take possession, make improvements, evict tenants or move onto the property. Gwinnett says buyers at a sale do not automatically own the property and owners are not immediately evicted.

The purchaser can end the owner's right to redeem only by following the notice rules in 48-4-45. After 12 months the purchaser serves notice on the defendant in the execution, the occupant, and everyone with a recorded interest or lien in the county, and must publish it once a week for four consecutive weeks in the sheriff's advertisement newspaper. Notice to people outside the county goes by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery.

Even then the deed is not final overnight. Under 48-4-48 a tax deed executed at a valid sale after July 1, 1996 ripens into fee simple title four years after the deed is recorded in the county land records.

What if I redeem the property or the sale brings in extra money?

Redemption puts the title back in the owner, subject to every lien that existed at the time of the sale, according to 48-4-43. The purchaser must then sign a quitclaim deed to the owner under 48-4-44, naming who paid the redemption money. If it is not presented at redemption, the purchaser has seven days to supply one properly witnessed, and it must reach the clerk of the superior court within ten days of the redemption. Our quitclaim deed guide explains that kind of deed.

When a sale brings in more than taxes and costs, the extra money belongs to the parties with an interest. Cobb says its tax commissioner may file an interpleader in superior court to distribute it, and DeKalb holds excess funds until a rightful party files a claim. DeKalb accepts claims only from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and not from an agent under a power of attorney.

How does the court-supervised sale differ?

Counties and cities that adopt the process under 48-4-76 can foreclose through superior court instead. The sale is advertised as sheriffs' sales are, cannot occur earlier than 45 days after the court's order, and the minimum bid is the redemption amount.

The owner's redemption window is shorter, 60 days after the sale, and the owner redeems by paying the minimum bid price into the superior court. Within 90 days after the sale, the petitioner must deliver the deed and file a report of the sale. Any surplus above the minimum bid is deposited with the court and distributed by priority to the interested parties, including the owner.

Can I sell my Georgia house before a tax sale?

Yes, a sale to a buyer that closes before the auction can pay the delinquent taxes out of the proceeds. The county will treat payment of everything owed as a stop to the sale, and Gwinnett confirms that the owner can pay all taxes, costs and fees after a property is selected for sale, in certified funds. Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff figure through your closing date, since advertising and title research fees keep being added as the sale approaches.

If the auction has already taken place, the 12 month redemption period is the next deadline. A buyer purchasing from you then has to account for the purchaser's rights as well, so involve a Georgia real estate attorney and a title company early.

More questions about Georgia Tax Sales

Where are Georgia tax sales held?

At the county, usually at the courthouse. DeKalb holds them on the courthouse steps in Decatur, Cobb at the Superior Court Plaza, and Gwinnett in front of the Justice and Administration Center in Lawrenceville.

How long do I have to redeem after a Georgia tax sale?

At least 12 months from the sale date. After that the right continues until the purchaser cuts it off by giving the statutory foreclosure notice to the owner, the occupant and recorded interest holders.

What does redemption cost?

The purchaser's bid, plus later taxes the purchaser paid, special assessments, and a premium of 20 percent for the first year or fraction and 10 percent for each additional year or fraction. Notice costs may be added. Get the exact figure in writing.

Does the buyer at a tax sale own the house immediately?

No. The buyer holds a tax deed that works like a lien until redemption rights end. Cobb says the purchaser cannot take possession, improve the property or evict tenants during that time.

What happens to extra money from a tax sale?

It is held for the parties entitled to it. DeKalb takes claims from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and Cobb may file an interpleader action in superior court to distribute the money.
